title: POC: Redwood SDK + OpenAI-Compat Integration Planning - Nova Fintech
summary: Initial scoping to define success criteria, workloads for benchmarks, and integration plan for OpenAI-compatible endpoints and SDK usage. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private options; strong emphasis on function/tool calling and structured JSON outputs for downstream processing. Next steps include benchmark worksheet, security packet, and scheduling a 2-hour technical deep dive to run sample load tests.

transcript:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:05] Raj (Nova Eng Lead): Raj here. Maya, Chris, Ellen with me.
[00:09] Alex: Great. We're here to scope the POC — specifically the integration path with our SDKs and the OpenAI-compatible endpoints, plus how you want function/tool calling and structured JSON outputs to look.
[01:02] Sienna (Redwood SE): Hi all. I'll take the tech lead today for the deep parts. High level: we want to make sure the POC validates three things: latency for interactive workflows, cost per 1M tokens range under your expected concurrency, and fidelity of structured outputs for downstream ingestion.
[01:36] Maya (Product): For us, success means the model outputs a reliable JSON payload for our transaction categorization pipeline with >95% entity extraction accuracy and tail latency under 300ms for 90th percentile.
[02:12] Alex: Good explicit metrics. Raj, current traffic and concurrency?
[02:18] Raj: We're seeing bursts up to 120 QPS on our classification endpoint, avg payload 350 tokens in and 120 tokens out. For the POC we can target a smaller slice — maybe 10 QPS sustained, peak 40 QPS to simulate spikes.
[02:46] Sienna: OK that maps well. For benchmarking we'll run three profile runs: low (10 QPS), med (40 QPS), and peak (120 QPS) focusing on p95 latency, tokens/sec, and cost/1k tokens. We'll also enable prefix caching on known templates to see cost savings.
[03:11] Chris (Security): On private/security: we need to know data residency options, KMS integrations, and audit log retention. Are you able to run a private control plane or VPC?
[03:28] Diego (Solutions Engineer): Yes, Redwood Private supports customer VPC and KMS/HSM integrations; we have audit logs and configurable retention. For the POC we can run in a dedicated sandbox VPC with RBAC and SAML SSO if you want.
[03:45] Chris: Good — please include SOC2 and ISO docs in the packet.
[04:02] Alex: We'll share our security packet. Back to integration: Maya, what SDKs are you planning to use? Server-side Node, python?
[04:12] Maya: Primary backend is Python (FastAPI), some Node microservices. We want the simplest path — OpenAI-compatible endpoints would let us switch with minimal code change.
[04:28] Sienna: Our OpenAI-compat layer supports both the chat/completions schema and function calling. We also expose a native SDK that wraps extended features like structured output enforcement and KV cache controls. If you use the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, function calling should still work, but advanced options like automatic prefix KV caching are accessible via our SDK flags.
[04:57] Raj: Are there differences in latency/cost between using the raw HTTP OpenAI-compatible endpoint and your SDK?
[05:03] Diego: Minimal for single requests; the SDK gives better batching and reuse of persistent connections which helps at higher concurrency. For cost there is parity at the model level, but SDK-enabled batching and cache reduce token consumption and therefore cost.
[05:34] Maya: We also rely on structured JSON outputs — sometimes nested objects for entities. How do you handle schema validation and hallucination mitigation?
[05:45] Sienna: We recommend a two-layer approach: model-level structured prompts (templates + few-shot examples) plus runtime schema enforcement with our structured output helper which can do best-effort correction and confidence scoring. During the POC we'll measure schema adherence percent and put a small validation harness in front of your pipeline.
[06:18] Raj: For benchmarks, what metric set do you usually give?
[06:22] Sienna: We'll provide p50/p90/p95 latencies, throughput (tokens/sec), cost per 1k tokens, token utilization (wasted tokens due to bad prompts), and structured-output F1 for entity extraction. We'll run with and without quantized models, and include CPU/GPU utilization charts.
[06:45] Maya: Quantized models — are those available on hosted? Any accuracy tradeoffs we should expect?
[06:51] Diego: We have quantized variants for several open models; typical small accuracy delta (<2-5%) but big cost savings. We'll run quality regressions with your prompt set to highlight tradeoffs.
[07:20] Chris: On logging and auditing — can we get token-level tracing for debugging but redact PII automatically?
[07:27] Alex: Yes, we can provide tracing with redaction rules. We'll include token-level cost breakdown in the console but redact content per policy.
[07:45] Maya: On function calling: our processors expect deterministic outputs to call internal APIs. How deterministic is function calling across retries?
[07:56] Sienna: Function calling is deterministic if you freeze model temperature and use the same function schema. For retries we recommend idempotent handlers or passing a request-id. We'll show an example during the tech deep dive.
[08:20] Raj: Timeline: We're targeting a decision by end of May. Can you run a 3-week POC with benchmarks in first two weeks and a final evaluation week?
[08:32] Alex: That's doable. We typically propose a 3-week POC: Week 0 (kickoff + infra + security review), Week 1 (integration + baseline runs), Week 2 (scale and regression testing), Week 3 (analysis + findings + recommendation). We can compress if needed.
[09:00] Maya: Budget/price expectations?
[09:03] Alex: We'll draft an estimate for a small reserved capacity + hosted usage for the POC. Pricing options: hosted pay-as-you-go, short reserved capacity for predictable throughput, or Dedicated nodes if you want strict isolation. We'll include cost projections per your projected QPS.
[09:32] Raj: For the POC can we use the OpenAI-compat API first to speed integration and then move to SDK features?
[09:40] Sienna: Yes, that's a common pattern — start with OpenAI-compat to validate outputs, then add the SDK to enable caching/batching and structured-output helpers.
[09:55] Ellen (ML Eng): Any code samples?
[09:58] Diego: We'll share a min repo with Python and Node examples showing OpenAI-compat calls, an SDK example that enables KV cache and batching, plus a function-calling sample. We'll also include a small harness to measure latency and p95 under load.
[10:18] Maya: On evaluation metrics — we want to track false positives on entity extraction. Will you run automated scoring?
[10:25] Sienna: Yes, provide your labeled ground truth and we'll run automated scoring across runs and generate a regression alert if performance drops more than 3%.
[10:38] Raj: Are there any gotchas with rate limits or concurrency?
[10:42] Diego: For hosted accounts we enforce a default rate limit; during POC we can lift those for the test window. Dedicated provides guaranteed throughput. You should also design clients to handle 429s and exponential backoff.
[11:03] Maya: For structured output, can we force JSON schema validation and reject outputs that don't comply?
[11:09] Sienna: Yes — the SDK has a strict mode that rejects or requests re-generation until schema is satisfied, with a configurable retry limit. We'll discuss costs of retries in the worksheet.
[11:30] Raj: Let's talk about benchmarks specifics. We want to run: 1) single-shot classification, 2) multi-turn assistant call with function invocation, 3) batch embedding runs for similarity search.
[11:44] Sienna: We'll create 3 benchmark suites: classification (your 350-in/120-out median), assistant with function-calling (simulate end-to-end API calls), and bulk embeddings. For embeddings we'll test throughput on dedicated smaller instances to get latency per 1k embeddings and cost curves.
[12:10] Alex: Any legal/procurement hurdles we should preempt?
[12:15] Chris: We'll need a contract addendum for data handling, plus export controls clearance. SAML SSO and RBAC are must-haves.
[12:26] Alex: Noted — we'll loop in legal.
[12:34] Maya: One more thing: we have an internal orchestrator that expects function outputs as flat arrays, not nested. Can the structured-output helper flatten schemas?
[12:44] Sienna: Yes, it can transform and flatten according to a mapping file. Please add a sample mapping to your prompt data.
[13:00] Raj: For the POC's technical deep dive — who should attend from your side?
[13:04] Alex: Sienna, Diego, and me. We'll bring a small infra setup and run a bench with your sample prompts.
[13:15] Maya: Great. Can you provide a checklist of infra requirements?
[13:19] Diego: We'll include SSH keys, VPC peering info for Private, and a minimal ingest endpoint.
[13:27] Alex: Quick recap — deliverables we'll send: POC scope doc + pricing, benchmark worksheet, SDK example repo, security/compliance packet, and schedule for tech deep dive.
[13:40] Maya: Sounds good.
[13:45] Chris: One question — do you support bring-your-own-model? We run a licensed model internally sometimes.
[13:52] Diego: On Redwood Private yes, you can bring your own model image and we can run it in your control plane. For hosted we can host custom models via a managed onboarding path, but we'd need licensing confirmation.
[14:14] Raj: OK let's lock dates: kickoff early week of 2025-04-14?
[14:19] Alex: We can do 2025-04-14 for kickoff. We'll send calendar invites after this call.
[14:27] Maya: Thanks everyone.
[14:30] Alex: Thanks — we'll follow up with the materials.
[14:34] (meeting ends)
notes: Customer wants >95% structured extraction and p95 <300ms for interactive flows
Plan: 3-week POC with progressive scale profiles
Start with OpenAI-compatible endpoints, then enable SDK features for batching/caching
